uncertainties.summary: Page 123 continues the October procession, its flour wagons, and bread imagery, but does not itself identify the crowd specifically as market women.
Page 191 treats the Prussian advance, front-line panic, and France's wartime crisis, but it does not identify an Austrian role on this page.
Page 192 treats French volunteering and the battle of Valmy against Prussian forces; Austria is not part of the action described on this page.
Page 180 places Robespierre in the war narrative but records only his criticism of Dumouriez's showy liberty-cap display.
Page 223 discusses price rises and supply disruption for sugar, soap, coffee, candles, and West Indian commodities, but calls them basic commodities rather than luxury goods.
Page 389 refers generally to victorious peace treaties before the legislature; the Peace of Amiens is named on page 390.
Page 370 ends with Barras's name but postpones every informative statement about him until page 371.
Page 387 substantively asks how bishops would be appointed and describes government designation, but does not state clerical election on this page.
Page 387 discusses future episcopal selection by state appointment, not an election of clergy on that page.
Page 387 describes the two rival episcopal bodies and the settlement problem but does not yet identify refractory priests explicitly.
Page 417 completes the cross-page statement that the French example reinforced patriotism in long-united states such as the Dutch Republic.
Page 420 reports that Théroigne de Méricourt was suspected of spying for “the emperor”; in the 1792 setting this refers to Francis II.
Page 413 treats the Revolution’s effects on Italian city-republics and begins the broader discussion of French remaking of Europe continued on page 414.
The supported October Days locator on page 123 was not accepted as a realistic lookup route to the distinct thematic claim that Paris became the Revolution's self-appointed guardian.

Page 126 is retrieved through the broader supported heading 'municipal authorities'; this was accepted as a realistic route to elected commune government, although the heading does not name communes explicitly.

The page-130 seigneurialism route was accepted as access to aristocratic resistance, but it does not itself connect that treatment to noble emigration, so the synthesized reader task remains only partially successful.
The full interpretation is distributed between Committee-of-Public-Safety and Law-of-14-Frimaire routes rather than one consolidated Revolutionary Government route.
Page 258 is reachable through Nantes, Carrier, and provincial-Terror routes rather than the Vendée-suppression subdivision itself.
The page-263 governing treatment is reachable through the Committee's dechristianization-policy subdivision, a narrower route than the frozen leadership-and-power subject.
A black-market entry reaches page 269, but it is too indirect to count as access to the frozen controlled-economy interpretation; that boundary judgment is medium confidence.
Desmoulins and moderate-newspaper entries reach page 269, but neither is an adequate first route to the frozen Danton-and-Indulgents subject.
Page 263 is reached through the Committee's dechristianization-policy subdivision rather than an explicit liberty-of-cults route.
The exact Defenders heading conflates the Irish agrarian Defenders with the French Defenders of the One and Indivisible Republic; broader Ireland and United Irishmen paths still retrieve page 341.

Registered locator review supports 5,123 of 5,338 atomic assignments; display-to-atomic ownership remains exact for all 4462 delivered displays.
All four substitutive ‘see’ references resolve to substantive access without self-reference, cycles, chains, or loss of warranted direct access; ten additional see-also routes are fully supported.

Alphabetical navigation is coherent apart from conventional punctuation/name-order comparisons (8 machine flags reviewed as non-defects); mechanical faults are localized to the recorded accent substitutions and registered MEC findings.
